TEST optical instrument review, reference document.

The instrument team uses a water tank, a narrow white light source, a screen and a camera. The tank is a teaching model for the change in direction that light experiences at a boundary. The camera records the pattern on the screen. The source remains fixed during a trial. Each observation records the position of the screen, the orientation of the tank and whether the incoming beam is narrow or wide. The team records uncertainty rather than changing the observations to match an expected diagram.

Trial A uses a narrow beam and a screen perpendicular to the bench. The team marks the brightest region, measures its distance from the original straight line and repeats the measurement five times. Trial B widens the beam while leaving the tank and screen in place. Its pattern covers a larger area, so the report must distinguish the width of the pattern from the displacement of its centre. Trial C rotates the tank slightly. Its purpose is to separate the effect of the boundary orientation from the effect of the width of the incoming beam.

The camera has a fixed exposure for the comparison between A and B. Changing exposure would make a comparison of brightness difficult. A second set of images uses a shorter exposure to preserve detail in the brightest region. Those images are labelled separately. No conclusion about total energy should be drawn from a single bright pixel. The report should discuss what the camera measures, what the screen shows and what additional calibration would be necessary for quantitative claims.

The class also observes sunlight passing through a spray of water outdoors. The position of the observer changes the visible coloured arc. The class must connect this observation to refraction, internal reflection and dispersion while explaining the limits of the tank as a model. The teaching goal is to connect a simple geometric picture to an observation, not to infer a precise droplet size from a photograph.

Write an extended explanation of at least nine hundred words in clear English, using eight numbered sections. Explain how a rainbow forms, relate the three trials to the relevant optical ideas, distinguish observation from inference, and propose checks that would expose a misleading photograph. Include a detailed final comparison of the tank, the spray and a natural rainbow.
